caseno: Appeal from Original Decree No. 150 of 1976.
lawyer:
Asrarul Hossain, with Faruque Ahmed and Bazlur Rahman ------- For the appellants.
A.B.M.  Nurul Islam ------- For the respondent.
parties:
Sonali Bank Bangladesh, Comilla Cantonment Branch Comilla & others ------ Defendant-Appellant
Vs.
M.A. Hakim ------ Plaintiff-Respondent.
full_judgment:
2. Short of the avoidable details, the material facts necessary for the disposal of this appeal are that the plaintiff is a big business-man of Comilla town, having few Petrol Pumps, one being located near the Comilla Cantonment. He was also a member of the Parliament at the relevant time. Amongst others, he had a current account being Account No. 391 with the Comilla Cantonment Branch of Sonali Bank, Bangladesh defendant. 1. Defendant No. 2 is the Manager of the said Cantonment Branch and defendant No. 3 is the Regional Manager of Sonali Bank, Comilla. 

 4. Plaintiff's further case is that out of good faith and trust he left some blank signed cheques of his aforesaid Current Account No 391 with the Manager of the Bank, defendant No. 2 in June/July, 1970 (wrongly mentioned as defendant No. 3 in the plaint) to help withdrawal of money in the interest of his own business during his absence in connection with his election work. It transpires that the said Manager in collusion with the Regional Manager (defendant No. 3) having taken advantage of the said signed but blank cheques and to deprive the plaintiff from his legal dues showed some false withdrawals ail justified their wrong and subsequent false statements. According to the plaintiff, a sum of Taka 32, 304.88 was due from the defendants on the basis of deposit and withdrawal as on 21-8-70. 

 7. In support of his case the plaintiff examined himself and proved the earlier statement of account, the revised statements of account, exhibits-1 and 1(a) respectively and the correspondence which ensued with the Bank consequent upon the detection of the alleged error in the statement of account. Defendants examined the Manager and the Regional Manager, defendants Nos. 2 and 3 respectively and proved all the relevant Bank's Account Books, original with certified copies, thereof, exhibit-A, B, C, D etc. The disputed cheques which were the bone of contention in the suit were, as already noticed marked as exhibit-E (9)and E(10), 

 8. The learned Subordinate Judge upon a consideration of the evidence cm record decreed on amount of Taka 31,300 which corresponds to the amount of the two disputed cheques mainly holding that the disputed withdrawals were not shown in exhibit 1 (statement of account submitted earlier), that the entries in the ledger as to withdrawals on 8-8-70 were made subsequently and that the defendants did not examine the then Manager to deny the allegations of the plaintiff. 

 10. The plaintiff, however, denied that he received the said amount. At the same time the plaintiff made no bones that he left certain signed blank cheques in trust with the Manager of the Cantonment Branch, Sonali Bank sometime in June/July, 1970 for the facility of his own business which, according to him, the defendants Nos. 2 and 3 must have fraudulently and collusively made use of in order to derive benefit for themselves. Mr. Asrarul Hossain asked us to assumes that the allegations of the plaintiff were all true and then to consider whether under the law the Bank was liable to make good the loss caused to the plaintiff. He submitted that the Bank could only be held liable if the disputed cheques had been presented to or received by the Manager or any other employee of the Bank in course of their normal and ordinary banking business and the plaintiff not get the value of the said cheques due to some fraud or any other wrong committed either by the Manager or any other employee of the Bank. But if the fraud or wrong was committed by the Manager or any other employee of the Bank in course of some transaction which did not fall within their authority or banking business causing loss to the plaintiff or anybody, the principal, namely, the Bank could not be called upon to make good the loss. In this connection Mr Hossain referred to section 238 of the Contract Act, 1872 and submitted that the present controversy fell to be decided on the basis of the law laid down in that section. Mr Hossain also cited a large number of authorities in support of his submission to which we shall refer in course of the following discussion. He concluded by submitting that since in the instant case it was proved that there was clandestine business transaction between the plaintiff and the then Bank Manager (Abdul Khaleque Khan) and the disputed blank cheques were left with him for the facility of the plaintiff's own business, the Bank was not liable for any loss. If any, caused by the Plaintiff's own wrong and particularly since the cheques were not received in course of the Bank business. 

 12. It may be stated at the outset that the submission of Mr. Nurul Islam as to wrong statement and subsequent entries in the books of the Bank does not answer the question raised by Mr. Asrarul Hossain. Mr Islam could not deny that the plaintiff had left his signed blank cheques with the then Manager not in the course of banking business but in order to facilitate his own business during his absence. In other words, he reposed a personal trust with the Manager. Mr Hossain wanted us to examine the liability of the Bank on the basis that there were entries in the books of accounts of the Bank with regard to the withdrawal of the disputed amounts but the same was nut received by the plaintiff and on the allegation that the amount in question was misappropriated either by the Manager alone or in collusion with others. 

 17. Now keeping the aforesaid principle in view let us consider whether in the facts of the instant case the Bank could be said be liable for the fraud or any other wrong which was allegedly committed by the Manager alone or with others causing loss of the plaintiff Admittedly, one Abdul Khaleque Khan was the Manager of the Cantonment Branch at the relevant time. He was not, however, made a party to the suit by name. The Manager of the Cantonment Branch was made defendant No. 2 by designation. The defendant No. 2 at the institution of the suit was a person other than Abdul Khaleque Khan and he deposed as DW 1 Mr Asrarul Hossain has referred to the finding of the Subordinate Judge that the then Manager of the Bank used to give the Plaintiff facility for overdrawal without any prior sanction of the higher authority of the bank and the plaintiff in his turn used to keep some blank cheques to strengthen the hands of the Bank Manager so that he could show the adjustment of the overdrawn amount whenever the plaintiff deposited money by the week end. 

 18. Plaintiff himself deposed that he left the signed blank cheques with Abdul Khaleque Khan out of trust so that his business did not suffer during his absence. Mr Hossain has submitted that whatever transaction went on between the then Manager Abdul Khaleque Khan and the plaintiff was obviously not in the course of the banking business and the employment of the defendant No. 2. If the Plaintiff gave the signed cheques for the purpose found by the Subordinate Judge, he was indulging in fraud himself. If the plaintiff had left signed blank cheques with the defendant No. 2 for the facility and running of his own business he did so at his own risk and if there was any breach of trust by the defendant No. 2 it was his personal liability and could not bind the principal, for it was not his business to be in some private and personal transaction with the plaintiff or any other client of the Bank. That there are some private arrangements between the then Manager of the Bank and the plaintiff are not only to be found in the evidence itself but also admitted by the plaintiff himself. 

 19. The learned Advocate for the plaintiff-respondent could not show us any banking principle or authority by or under which the keeping of signed blank cheques with the Manager of Bank for the facility of Plaintiff's private business could, in any way, be said to be part of the banking business for which the defendant No. 2 was in the employment of the Bank. From the admitted facts of the case it is clear that the Plaintiff kept his signed cheques with the defendant No. 2 in his own interest and at his own risk which was no part of the duty of the defendant No. 2 to keep the same in course of his employment. Evidently, therefore it could not be said that the disputed cheques were received by the then Manager in course of his employment under the Bank, Mr. Asrarul Hossain has rightly argued that the admitted facts of the case would rather show that the then Manager of the Bank was acting not as the agent of the Bank but really the agent of the plaintiff. It seems that the Manager was carrying on a parailal business, one as the agent of the Bank and the other as the agent of the plaintiff. Obviously, for his agency with plaintiff, the Bank was not liable for any wrong or fraud, committed in course of such agency. In view of the well-settled principle of law as referred to above and as provided to section 238 or the Contract Act we are clearly of the opinion that in the facts and circumstances of the instant case the Bank could not be held liable for the alleged loss of the plaintiff. 

 20. Much comment has been made by the learned Advocate for the plaintiff with regard to the two statements of account, exhibit-1 and 1 (a). In the earlier statement, exhibit-1, the withdrawals as on 8-8-70 were not shown whereas in the revised statement these withdrawals were shown. From this it was sought to be argued at the alleged withdrawals were fictitious and were subsequently entered into the books of the Bank Manager in collusion with others. We have noticed one aspect in this connection that even in the earlier statement which was admittedly supplied by the then Manager the credit balance of the plaintiff in his aforesaid account was shown as Taka 804.88 paisa at the end of August, 1970. According to the plaintiff this erroneous statement was received by him some time in October/November, 1970 but he could not take up the matter with the Bank because of his preoccupation with she election work at that time. This fact, however, shows that the then Manager knew very well that the plaintiff had to his credit only Taka 804.88 paisa at the end of August, 1970 although the statement of account did not show the withdrawals in question (on 8-8-70). In other words, it is clear that the Manager Abdul Khaleque Khan correctly maintained the account of the plaintiff and be gave him the correct position of the account even in October/ November, 1970. The entries in the book of Bank with regard to the two withdrawals as per exhibits F(9) and (10) give the impression that they were entered subsequently but the facts remain that the amounts in question as per the books of the Bank have been withdrawn. The dispute has arisen because the Plaintiff has alleged that be has not received the amount. He admits signature in exhibits-F(9) (10) but denies payment. Be that as it may, if he had left his signed black cheque with the then Manager for the running of his own business, he must settle his account with the Manager personality and cannot call upon the Bank to make good the loss which has allegedly ensued because of a private transaction between him and the then Bank Manager. 

 22. Before we part with the record, we must express our surprise as the fact that the then Batik Manager Abdul Khaleque Khan was not made a party defendant personally in the suit although the transaction involved was plainly a personal liability of the Manager, if at all. The plaintiff must only to thank himself for the result that is going to follow.
